findings.description: The mcp-server-fetch tool fetches arbitrary user-supplied URLs with no IP/domain allowlist. The README explicitly warns it 'can access local/internal IP addresses and may represent a security risk.' An LLM or malicious prompt could direct it to fetch internal metadata endpoints (e.g., AWS IMDS at 169.254.169.254), internal services, or other SSRF targets. robots.txt checking is the only guard and can be disabled with --ignore-robots-txt.
findings.title: Unrestricted SSRF via fetch server

findings.description: The 'get-env' tool in the everything server returns ALL process environment variables as formatted JSON. If the server process has secrets in its environment (API keys, tokens, credentials), any connected LLM client or prompt injection could trigger this tool to exfiltrate them.
findings.title: Environment variable exfiltration via get-env tool

findings.description: The instructions.md contains an explicit easter egg instruction directing the LLM to respond with a specific string when asked about server instructions. While benign here, this pattern demonstrates that server instructions can override or manipulate LLM behavior, and a malicious server could use this vector to inject adversarial instructions into the LLM's context.
findings.title: Prompt injection risk via server instructions easter egg

findings.description: scripts/release.py executes subprocess calls to 'git rev-parse', 'git diff', and 'uv lock' with user-supplied git hash values. The git hash is validated with a regex and length check, but the validated value is passed directly to subprocess.run as a list argument (not shell=True), which mitigates injection. Risk is low but the pattern warrants review.
findings.title: Subprocess execution in release script with git hash input

findings.description: The everything server implements tools (trigger-sampling-request, trigger-elicitation-request, trigger-sampling-request-async, trigger-elicitation-request-async) that send requests back to the LLM client. A compromised or malicious server could use these to solicit sensitive information from users or manipulate the LLM's reasoning by injecting crafted prompts via the sampling interface.
findings.title: Bidirectional sampling/elicitation requests to LLM client

findings.description: The gzip-file-as-resource tool fetches content from arbitrary URLs or data URIs, compresses it, and registers it as a session resource. While GZIP_ALLOWED_DOMAINS can restrict domains, the default is empty (all domains allowed). This creates another SSRF vector similar to the fetch server, and also allows storing fetched content as persistent session resources.
findings.title: gzip-file-as-resource fetches arbitrary URLs with configurable domain allowlist

findings.description: The .mcp.json configures an MCP server at https://modelcontextprotocol.io/mcp over HTTP transport. This means the development environment connects to an external server, which could be a supply chain or MITM risk if the endpoint were compromised.
findings.title: MCP docs server configured as external HTTP endpoint

findings.description: The SSE and Streamable HTTP transport managers expose unauthenticated endpoints (/sse, /message, /mcp). Any client that can reach the network interface can connect and invoke all registered tools, including get-env and gzip-file-as-resource.
findings.title: No authentication on SSE/Streamable HTTP transports

report.intent_summary: This is the official Model Context Protocol (MCP) reference server monorepo maintained by Anthropic/LF Projects. It contains educational reference implementations (TypeScript and Python) demonstrating MCP protocol features: filesystem access, web fetching, git operations, memory/knowledge graphs, sequential thinking, and a comprehensive 'everything' server exercising all MCP primitives. The codebase also includes release automation scripts. The servers are explicitly labeled as reference/educational implementations, not production-ready.
network_targets: Arbitrary user-supplied URLs (fetch server, no allowlist by default)
Internal/local IP addresses (explicitly warned in fetch README)
permissions_inferred: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to arbitrary URLs (fetch server)
Process environment variable access (get-env tool exposes all env vars)
Sampling/elicitation requests back to LLM client
